idiom_name: typed DAO interface plus a class over pg.Pool (row generics, explicit row-to-domain mapping)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds what JavaScript lacks - a checked contract - so the DAO is an interface over row-typed queries (pg.Pool.query<CustomerRow>) plus a class whose only dependency is the injected pool, with mapping from row types to domain types happening inside the boundary. What replaces the classic structure is structural typing plus dependency injection: a second store is another class implementing the same interface, and tests substitute a fake without any framework. Keep this form while SQL stays hand-written; use the generated-client variant when the schema is the source of truth and per-model operations can be generated.
pitfalls: Type parameters on query results are erased at runtime: pool.query<CustomerRow> is a cast, not validation, so columns can still disagree with the declared row type - map explicitly and validate at the boundary.
Transactions need a checked-out client (pool.connect() with release in a finally block): splitting one transaction across pool.query calls silently runs statements on different connections.
The seam is only as real as the compiler settings: with strictNullChecks off, 'Customer | null' collapses and callers keep exactly the bugs the interface was meant to prevent.

variants.name: Schema-generated Prisma client as the DAO (typed per-model operations)
variants.idiom_name: generated client: db.orm.<Model>.where(...).all()/.first() (findMany/findUnique in older APIs)
variants.implementation_notes: Prisma realises Oracle's automatic code-generation strategy literally: models are declared once in the schema (contract) file and the generated client exposes typed per-model operations whose result types are derived from that schema, so SQL, pooling and row mapping are all hidden behind domain-named calls. The DAO layer then shrinks to a thin wrapper that re-exposes intent-revealing methods, which is exactly the split the pattern asks for; keep hand-written SQL DAOs when queries are too dynamic or vendor-specific for the generator to express. Trade-off versus the pool variant is a build step and a generated artefact coupled to every schema change.
variants.code_sketch:
import { db } from './prisma/db'   // client created once; types derive from the schema

export const customerDao = {        // domain-named facade over generated operations
  find: (id: string) => db.orm.public.Customer.first({ id }),
  byEmail: (email: string) => db.orm.public.Customer.where({ email }).all(),
  add: (c: NewCustomer) => db.orm.public.Customer.create(c),
};                                   // no SQL and no connection handling in this file
pitfalls: The generated client hides round trips as effectively as any ORM: calling the DAO inside a loop is an N+1 that the typed API makes look cheap.
Types follow the schema, so a migration regenerates them and compile errors surface far from the DAO; review schema changes as interface changes.
